Using the MNIST digits dataset, a systematic evaluation was performed based on accuracy, computational efficiency, and architectural complexity. The experimental results demonstrate that the Genetic Algorithm achieved the highest accuracy at 98.33%, while Grid Search demonstrated computational efficiency with the fastest execution time at just 31.06 seconds. Random Search and Adaptive Search showed competitive performance with accuracies of 97.78% and 97.22% respectively, with varying computational requirements. The study revealed that simpler architectures with one or two layers often performed comparably to more complex structures, challenging the common assumption that deeper networks necessarily yield better results. The Genetic Algorithm converged to an optimal single-layer architecture with 119 neurons and ReLU activation, while Adaptive Search explored a more complex three-layer solution. The research identified a non-linear relationship between accuracy gains and computational costs, indicating that substantial increases in computational investment may yield diminishing returns in performance improvement. The convergence patterns of each method provided additional insights, with GA showing steady improvement across generations while Random Search achieved early discovery of good solutions. These findings contribute to both theoretical understanding and practical applications of neural network optimization, offering valuable insights into the trade-offs between methods and practical guidelines for selecting appropriate architecture optimization strategies based on specific requirements for accuracy and computational The field has seen rapid advancements, driven by the need to optimize the trade-off between detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Among existing models, the YOLO family has emerged as a leading solution, offering a well-balanced performance that makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications on embedded systems.As detection tasks become more complex, choosing the right model for a given task becomes increasingly important. While newer architectures may show improved performance on standard benchmarks, older models can still outperform them in specialized scenarios. This highlights the necessity for efficient model selection tailored to specific task requirements.Neural Architecture Search (NAS) provides a promising approach to this problem by automating model design. However, the effectiveness of NAS largely depends on the quality and flexibility of the search space. In this paper, we propose a novel NAS technique that explores the search space in a hybrid manner combining both block-level and operation-level searches. Specifically, we introduce modular blocks as new search units and leverage components from YOLOv3 to YOLOv11 to construct a rich and diverse search space.Our method enables task-specific optimization by reusing proven modular blocks and operations, achieving an effective balance between speed and accuracy. We validate MBNAS on COCO and VisDrone datasets and demonstrate high-performing models optimized for deployment on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier board using
